content: Once the uterus is well-contracted, the placenta and membranes should be delivered by applying traction to all umbilical cords simultaneously. Before and after delivering the placenta and membranes, closely monitor for vaginal bleeding, as this woman is at an increased risk of postpartum hemorrhage. If the placenta is incomplete, refer to the appropriate guidelines. There may be one large placenta with two umbilical cords or separate placentas with one umbilical cord for each baby. Immediate Postpartum Care: Monitor the mother intensively due to the increased risk of bleeding. Provide immediate postpartum care as per established protocols. Keep the mother in the health facility for at least 24 hours after birth. Offer special support for the care and feeding of the babies. Care of the Mother and Newborn Within the First Hour After Delivery of the Placenta: Use a structured chart to guide care during the first hour after the placenta is delivered. Assess the newborn’s breathing by listening for grunting and observing for chest in-drawing or rapid breathing. Check the newborn’s warmth by feeling if the feet are cold to the touch. Examine the umbilical cord for oozing and assess the baby’s sucking and feeding ability. Record all findings, treatments, and procedures in the labor record and partograph. Keep the mother and baby together in the delivery room and do not separate them. Never leave the mother and newborn alone. Interventions for the Mother: Assess the amount of vaginal bleeding. Encourage the mother to eat and drink. If the uterus is soft, manage it as per established guidelines. If bleeding is due to a perineal tear, repair it or refer the mother to a hospital if necessary. Interventions for the Newborn: Wipe the baby’s eyes and apply an antimicrobial ointment (e.g., tetracycline) to both eyes once, following national guidelines. Do not wash away the antimicrobial. If there is blood or meconium on the baby, wipe it off with a wet cloth and dry the baby. Do not remove vernix or bathe the baby. Keep the baby warm and in skin-to-skin contact with the mother. Encourage the mother to initiate breastfeeding when the baby shows readiness, and offer assistance if needed. If the baby has difficulty breathing (e.g., grunting, chest in-drawing, or rapid breathing), examine the baby further. Postpartum Monitoring and Care: Monitor the mother at 2, 3, and 4 hours postpartum, then every 4 hours. Check for emergency signs using rapid assessment protocols. Record all findings, treatments, and procedures in the labor record and partograph. Keep the mother and baby together and do not discharge them before 24 hours. Postpartum Interventions if Required: Accompany the mother and baby to the ward. Advise on postpartum care and hygiene. Encourage the mother to eat, drink, and rest. If the mother is HIV-infected, provide appropriate treatment and prophylaxis. If there is heavy vaginal bleeding, palpate the uterus. If the uterus is not firm, massage the fundus to encourage contraction and expel clots. If the bleeding is severe, manage as per established guidelines and refer to a hospital if necessary. If she cannot pass urine or the bladder is full, assist her by gently pouring water on the vulva. Avoid catheterization unless absolutely necessary. Postpartum Nutrition and Hygiene: Advise the mother to eat a greater variety and quantity of healthy foods, such as meat, fish, oils, nuts, seeds, cereals, beans, vegetables, cheese, and milk, to help her recover and maintain strength. Spend additional time on nutrition counseling for very thin women and adolescents. Address any cultural food taboos that may prevent the mother from consuming nutritious foods. Family Planning and Birth Spacing: Counsel the mother on the importance of family planning and discuss options with her and her partner if appropriate. Explain that if she is not exclusively breastfeeding, she can become pregnant as early as four weeks after delivery. Encourage her to consider a family planning method early. Advise waiting at least two years before attempting another pregnancy for the health of both the mother and baby. Provide information on family planning methods suitable for breastfeeding and non-breastfeeding women. Danger Signs and Emergency Preparedness: Advise the mother to seek immediate medical care if she experiences any of the following: Vaginal bleeding that soaks more than 2-3 pads in 20-30 minutes or increases rather than decreases. Convulsions. Severe headache with blurred vision. Rapid or difficult breathing. Fever and extreme weakness. Severe abdominal pain. Calf pain, redness, or swelling, or chest pain. Discuss emergency preparedness with the mother and her family, including where to go, how to get there, costs involved, and available support. Postpartum Follow-Up: Schedule routine postnatal contacts: First contact within 24 hours after childbirth. Second contact on day 3 (48-72 hours). Third contact between days 7 and 14 after birth. Advise the mother to return for follow-up care and to bring her partner or family member to at least one visit.
